Results from spectroscopic observations of the Intermediate Polar (IP) EX Hya in quiescence during 1991 and 2001 are presented. Spin-modulated radial velocities consistent with an outer disc origin were detected for the first time in an IP. The spin pulsation was modulated with velocities near ~500-600 km/s. These velocities are consistent with those of material circulating at the outer edge of the accretion disc, suggesting corotation of the accretion curtain with material near the Roche lobe radius. Furthermore, spin Doppler tomograms have revealed evidence of the accretion curtain emission extending from velocities of ~500 km/s to ~1000 km/s. These findings have confirmed the theoretical model predictions of King & Wynn (1999), Belle et al. (2002) and Norton et al. (2004) for EX Hya, which predict large accretion curtains that extend to a distance close to the Roche lobe radius in this system. Evidence for overflow stream of material falling onto the magnetosphere was observed, confirming the result of Belle et al. (2005) that disc overflow in EX Hya is present during quiescence as well as outburst. It appears that the hbeta and hgamma spin radial velocities originated from the rotation of the funnel at the outer disc edge, while those of halpha were produced due to the flow of material along the field lines far from the white dwarf (narrow component) and close to the white dwarf (broad-base component), in agreement with the accretion curtain model.

# Spectroscopic Observations of the Intermediate Polar EX Hydrae in Quiescence

Spectroscopic observations of the Intermediate Polar (IP) EX Hydrae, conducted during quiescence in 1991 and 2001, revealed spin-modulated radial velocities that were consistent with an outer disc origin. This finding was significant as it represented the first time such an origin had been identified in an Intermediate Polar, offering new insights into the accretion geometry of these systems.

The spin pulsation exhibited modulation with velocities in the range of approximately 500–600 km/s. These velocities suggest that the accretion curtain corotates with material located near the Roche lobe radius, at the outer edge of the accretion disc. This behaviour points to a coupling between the magnetically confined accretion flow and the outermost regions of the disc, providing important constraints on the physical scale of the accretion structures within the system.

Further analysis using spin Doppler tomograms showed accretion curtain emission extending from approximately 500 km/s to 1000 km/s. This broad velocity range confirmed theoretical model predictions that the accretion curtains in such systems are large, reaching close to the Roche lobe radius. The agreement between the observed tomographic structure and the predictions of accretion curtain models lends strong support to our understanding of how material is channelled onto the white dwarf in Intermediate Polars.

In addition, the observations provided evidence for an overflow stream of material falling directly onto the magnetosphere. This finding confirmed that disc overflow in EX Hydrae occurs not only during outburst, as had been previously established, but also during quiescence. The persistence of this overflow across different accretion states has important implications for models of mass transfer and accretion in these systems.

Finally, the origins of the different spectral line velocities were identified and interpreted within the framework of the accretion curtain model. The Hβ and Hγ spin radial velocities were found to originate from the rotation of the accretion funnel at the outer disc edge. In contrast, the Hα velocities were produced by material flowing along magnetic field lines, both far from and close to the white dwarf. This distinction between the line-forming regions is fully consistent with the accretion curtain model, reinforcing its validity as a description of the accretion processes at work in EX Hydrae.

# Spin-Modulated Radial Velocities and Accretion Structure in EX Hydrae

## Introduction

EX Hydrae is one of the most well-studied intermediate polars, a subclass of magnetic cataclysmic variables in which a magnetized white dwarf accretes material from a Roche-lobe-filling companion star. In these systems, the magnetic field of the white dwarf is strong enough to disrupt the inner accretion disc but not so strong as to prevent disc formation entirely. As a result, accreting material is channeled along the field lines onto the magnetic poles of the white dwarf, forming curved structures known as accretion curtains. Understanding the geometry and behavior of these curtains is essential for constraining models of accretion physics in magnetic systems.

## Observations and Methods

To investigate the accretion structure of EX Hydrae, spectroscopic observations obtained during quiescence in two separate epochs, 1991 and 2001, were analyzed. These observations spanned the spin period of the white dwarf, allowing the study of how emission-line radial velocities vary as the white dwarf rotates. The primary analytical technique employed was Doppler tomography, a powerful method that reconstructs the velocity-space distribution of line-emitting material in the binary system. By mapping emission into velocity coordinates, Doppler tomography enables the identification of distinct accretion components, such as the accretion disc, the gas stream, and regions where material overflows the disc.

## Results

The analysis revealed spin-modulated radial velocities with amplitudes on the order of approximately 500 to 1000 km/s. The magnitude and phasing of these velocities are consistent with an origin in the outer regions of the accretion disc, rather than in material located close to the white dwarf surface. This finding provides direct observational support for theoretical predictions that the accretion curtains in EX Hydrae are unusually large, extending outward to distances approaching the Roche lobe radius of the white dwarf. Such extended curtains distinguish EX Hydrae from many other intermediate polars, in which the magnetospheric radius is considerably smaller.

In addition to confirming the large-scale accretion curtain geometry, the Doppler tomography analysis revealed evidence for disc overflow during quiescence. Disc overflow occurs when part of the accretion stream from the companion star passes over or through the outer edge of the disc rather than being fully absorbed into it, allowing material to impact the magnetosphere directly. The detection of this component during the quiescent state indicates that overflow accretion is an ongoing feature of the system and not limited to periods of enhanced mass transfer.

## Conclusion

Taken together, the detection of spin-modulated velocities consistent with an outer disc origin, combined with the identification of disc overflow, validates existing accretion curtain models for EX Hydrae. These results confirm the theoretical picture of a system in which large accretion curtains reach outward toward the Roche lobe radius, and they reinforce our understanding of how magnetically channeled accretion operates in intermediate polars. The consistency between the observational data from both epochs and the model predictions demonstrates the robustness of the accretion curtain framework as applied to this important benchmark system.

# Understanding Intermediate Results in Polar Studies

When conducting research in polar environments, scientists rarely arrive at conclusions in a single step. Instead, the path toward reliable findings passes through a series of **intermediate** stages, each producing partial data that shape the direction of the work.

## The Value of Intermediate Findings

Intermediate results are the preliminary outcomes gathered before a study is complete. In **polar** research—whether examining ice sheets, ocean currents, or atmospheric conditions—these early observations are crucial. They help researchers adjust their methods, identify unexpected patterns, and refine their hypotheses before committing to final conclusions.

For example, a team studying Arctic sea ice may collect measurements over several seasons. The **results** from the first season serve as an intermediate benchmark, offering clues about long-term trends while highlighting gaps that require further investigation.

## From Polar Observations to Conclusions

Polar regions present unique challenges: extreme cold, remote locations, and rapidly changing conditions. Because of this, gathering complete data can take years. Reporting **intermediate results** allows the scientific community to stay informed and to build upon ongoing work rather than waiting for a distant final report.

These staged findings also improve accuracy. By reviewing intermediate data, researchers can catch errors early, calibrate their instruments, and ensure that the final **results** rest on a solid foundation.

## Conclusion

In polar science, progress is built step by step. Intermediate results act as guideposts, transforming raw observations into meaningful knowledge. By valuing each stage of discovery, researchers ensure that their final conclusions about our planet's polar regions are both reliable and insightful.

# Abstract

We present time-resolved spectroscopic observations of the intermediate polar EX Hydrae obtained during quiescence, aimed at characterizing the spin-modulated emission arising from the accretion curtains. High-resolution spectra covering the Balmer and He II λ4686 emission lines were acquired over multiple spin cycles of the white dwarf (P_spin ≈ 67 min), enabling a detailed analysis of the velocity structure of the accretion flow. We measured radial velocity variations that exhibit clear modulation on the white dwarf spin period, with an amplitude and phasing consistent with emission originating in the magnetically confined accretion curtains rather than in the accretion disk or bright spot. Doppler tomography reveals emission distributed along the predicted trajectories of material threading onto the magnetic field lines, supporting the accretion curtain model in which infalling gas is channeled toward the magnetic poles. The observed S-wave components and their velocity amplitudes are used to constrain the radial extent of the magnetosphere and the geometry of the accretion region. We find that the peak emission velocities are consistent with material corotating near the boundary between the disk and the magnetosphere, providing an estimate of the magnetospheric radius that is comparable to the corotation radius—a defining characteristic of EX Hya as a near-equilibrium rotator. The line ratios and their spin-phase dependence indicate optically thick conditions at the base of the curtains. These results reinforce the picture of EX Hya as a system in which accretion proceeds through extended curtains, and they offer observational constraints relevant to models of magnetically controlled accretion in cataclysmic variables with short spin-to-orbital period ratios.

---

# Spectroscopic Observations of Disc Overflow and Accretion Curtains in Intermediate Polars

## Background: Intermediate Polars

Intermediate polars (IPs) are magnetic cataclysmic variables where a moderately magnetized white dwarf accretes material from a Roche-lobe-filling companion star. The magnetic field is strong enough to disrupt the inner accretion disc but weak enough that a disc can partially form—creating a hybrid accretion geometry that spectroscopy is well-suited to probe.

## Disc Overflow vs. Pure Disc Accretion

A central question in IP studies concerns **how material actually reaches the magnetosphere**. Two main scenarios exist:

1. **Disc-fed accretion**: Material circularizes into a disc, then couples to field lines at the magnetospheric radius.

2. **Stream-fed / disc overflow accretion**: Part of the accretion stream from the L1 point overflows the disc plane and impacts the magnetosphere directly, without full circularization.

### Spectroscopic Signatures

Spectroscopy reveals these processes through **radial velocity variations and emission line behavior**:

- **Emission lines** (particularly the Balmer series and He II λ4686) show velocity components modulated on both the **orbital period** and the **spin period** of the white dwarf.
- The presence of velocity modulation at the **beat period** (between spin and orbit) is a key diagnostic of **disc overflow**, since it indicates that accretion is partly phase-locked to the orbital geometry rather than purely to the rotating magnetosphere.
- **Doppler tomography** maps emission in velocity space, allowing separation of disc, stream, and magnetospheric components.

## The King & Wynn Model

**King & Wynn** developed theoretical frameworks addressing the **equilibrium spin state** and accretion geometry of IPs:

- They modeled how the white dwarf's spin adjusts so that material is accreted near the **corotation radius**, establishing a **spin equilibrium**.
- Their work explored the balance between disc-fed and stream-fed accretion, predicting conditions under which **overflow streams** can dominate.
- The model helps explain why some IPs show strong stream-related spectroscopic signatures while others appear more disc-dominated.

## Norton's Accretion Curtain Models

**Norton and collaborators** advanced the concept of **accretion curtains**:

- As material couples onto magnetic field lines at the magnetospheric radius, it forms **arc-shaped curtains** of infalling gas following the dipolar field toward the magnetic poles.
- These curtains produce characteristic **spin-modulated emission and absorption** as they rotate into and out of the line of sight.
- Norton's models predict the **velocity structure** of the curtains—material accelerates as it falls, producing broad, spin-phase-dependent line profiles.
- The models distinguish observational signatures based on the **degree of magnetism and accretion mode**, linking spin-pulse behavior to curtain geometry.

## EX Hydrae as a Case Study

**EX Hya** is one of the best-studied IPs and a benchmark for these models:

- It has an unusually **long spin-to-orbital period ratio** (Pspin/Porb ≈ 0.68), placing it near a special regime where the magnetospheric radius approaches the **circularization radius** or even the orbital-related length scales.
- **Spectroscopic observations** reveal emission lines with velocity components consistent with **accretion curtains**, showing material moving at velocities near the white dwarf.
- The **spin-modulated radial velocities** of the Balmer and He II lines are interpreted as arising from the rotating curtains, matching Norton-type predictions.
- Some studies find evidence relevant to the **King & Wynn** picture where EX Hya's magnetospheric radius may extend toward the Roche lobe scale, making it an important test of whether it accretes primarily from a disc or through a more direct coupling.

### What EX Hya Specifically Demonstrates

- The **velocity amplitude** of spin-modulated lines constrains the location where material couples to the field.
- Line profile variations across the spin cycle map the **rising and falling curtain arcs**.
- Comparison with model predictions helps establish that EX Hya's accretion is **disc-fed with curtain-dominated inner accretion**, though its extreme parameters make it a distinctive rather than typical example.

## Summary

Spectroscopy—through radial velocities, line profiles, and Doppler tomography—reveals the **geometry and dynamics** of accretion in IPs. Modulations at the spin, orbital, and beat periods distinguish **disc overflow** from pure disc accretion, while line velocity structure traces the **accretion curtains** predicted by Norton. The **King & Wynn** framework provides the underlying spin-equilibrium and accretion-mode context. **EX Hya** serves as a key testbed because its extreme period ratio pushes these models into a revealing regime.

---

*Note: For precise quantitative details and the most current interpretations, I'd recommend consulting the primary literature (e.g., specific papers by Norton et al., King & Wynn, and spectroscopic studies of EX Hya), as my summary captures the general framework but specific observational values and their latest interpretations should be verified against source papers.*

# Balmer Line Radial Velocities in EX Hydrae

EX Hydrae is an intermediate polar (a magnetic cataclysmic variable) where the accretion flow is channeled by the white dwarf's magnetic field, making spectroscopic diagnostics of different Balmer lines valuable for probing distinct regions of the accretion structure. In studies of this system, the radial velocity variations of H-alpha, H-beta, and H-gamma modulated on the white dwarf spin period trace emission arising from material at different locations along the accretion curtains and flow. Because these hydrogen Balmer lines can form under somewhat different physical conditions of temperature, density, and optical depth, they tend to sample different depths and heights within the accretion column. The higher-order Balmer lines like H-gamma, which typically form in denser and hotter regions closer to the white dwarf surface near the accretion shock and post-shock cooling zone, can show radial velocity amplitudes and phase behavior that differ from H-alpha. H-alpha, being more optically thick and often produced in cooler, more extended regions of the accretion curtains farther from the white dwarf, may reflect the velocity field of material still magnetically threaded but at larger distances. The systematic phase shifts and amplitude differences observed between these lines therefore provide a way to map the velocity structure of the accretion flow, distinguishing contributions from the funneled magnetic curtains versus emission nearer the accretion region.
